transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Carter (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Sandpit Lead Engineer), Priya Nair (Sandpit DevOps), Samir Patel (Sandpit CTO)

Auto-generated summary: Intro SDK + auth + env demo, some network questions, next steps to share keys and schedule follow-up.

---Transcript body---
[00:00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, AE on the account. We got Maya from SE who will run the demo. Jordan, Priya, Samir, thanks for making time.
[00:00:12] Jordan: Hi Alex, hi Maya. Excited, we've skimmed the docs but want a hands-on on auth and CI patterns.
[00:00:18] Maya: Great, we'll walk through Python + TS quickstart, then environment & CI, then touch on Dedicated/VPC because you mentioned regulatory constraints earlier.
[00:00:31] Samir: Yes security is the big one for us — SOC2, KMS, and we may need Private if data residency becomes strict.
[00:00:40] Alex: Noted. We'll cover SSO and KMS integrations briefly and point you to our security deck.
[00:00:48] Maya: Ok starting the demo. First step is pip install redwood-sdk, or npm install @redwood/inference, we've got a public onboarding repo — I'll paste a link in the chat after.
[00:01:03] Maya: Python snippet: from redwood import Client; client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) — that's the typical pattern. Note that tokens are scoped to sandbox by default.
[00:01:17] Priya: Sandbox tokens, are they long lived? How do we rotate them in CI?
[00:01:23] Maya: Good question. Sandbox keys are long-lived for convenience but we recommend short-lived tokens for prod. We have a token exchange flow and examples for vault rotation. For CI, put the key in secrets manager and rotate every 30 days, or use ephemeral tokens via our session API.
[00:01:40] Jordan: You mentioned session API — is that part of the SDK?
[00:01:44] Maya: Yes, it's exposed via client.sessions.create() in the SDK; you can request ephemeral tokens that expire after a set TTL. There's a small server-side component that mints those using your long-lived service key.
[00:01:58] Alex: I'll add the server-side minting pattern to the repo we'll share.
[00:02:05] [00:02:05] Speaker 4: (inaudible)
[00:02:11] Maya: On env vars, we recommend REDWOOD_API_KEY in process.env or os.environ; for multi-env setups, prefix with ENV, e.g., REDWOOD_SANDBOX_KEY. For CI use secrets manager (GitHub Actions secrets, GitLab CI variables, or Vault).
[00:02:30] Priya: Any example GitHub Actions snippet?
[00:02:33] Maya: Yes — in the repo there's a workflow that sets REDWOOD_API_KEY from secrets and uses the SDK to run a smoke test. I can highlight that file.
[00:02:43] Jordan: What about rate limits? We plan to batch requests at inference layer.
[00:02:48] Maya: Hosted has soft rate limits in sandbox but for prod you can request higher quotas. Also consider batching at the SDK level — our client has a batch helper that aggregates short-lived requests. That reduces per-token overhead.
[00:03:02] Maya: Quick demo: TypeScript example — import Redwood from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); await client.generate({ model: 'rw-large-v1', input: 'summarize...' })
[00:03:18] Jordan: Model names — is rw-large-v1 Redwood's curated model?
[00:03:21] Alex: rw-large-v1 is one of our verified catalog entries; we'll include the model profile sheet with per-token latency and cost.
[00:03:29] Samir: How do we migrate between hosted and Dedicated? We may start hosted then move Dedicated.
[00:03:35] Maya: We provide the same API and SDK across modes. The main changes are the endpoint and keys. For Dedicated you get a different base URL and a dedicated credential. Rolling upgrades are also supported via rollout policies in Console.
[00:03:50] Jordan: Any infrastructure changes required on our side for Dedicated?
[00:03:54] Maya: Typically just VPC peering or egress rules if you want private networking. For on-prem Private we supply an installer, but that's a longer process. For Dedicated, you configure peering and we provide the IP allowlist.
[00:04:09] Priya: IP allowlist — can you give an example of the egress ports and IPs?
[00:04:13] Alex: We'll send the exact allowlist but usually HTTPS 443 to specific Redwood gateway IP ranges and optional tunneling for metrics. I'll add that to the follow-up email.
[00:04:23] Maya: Back to the SDK — I'm going to show a small local dev workflow: run with a lightweight token, switch to ephemeral tokens for staging, then to a service principal for prod.
[00:04:38] [00:04:38] Alex: Quick interruption — Jordan asked about streaming responses earlier in the ticket. Our SDK supports streaming with an event emitter pattern in Node and an async iterator in Python.
[00:04:51] Jordan: Good. We stream chat responses so we care about latency and partial tokens.
[00:04:56] Maya: In that case you can enable the streaming flag; it reduces perceived latency because you get tokens as generated. There's also a hooks API to push token deltas to the client.
[00:05:09] Priya: Any advice on token caching? We have repeated prompts with similar prefixes.
[00:05:14] Maya: We have built-in KV prefix caching in our Optimize product; for quick wins you can implement a local cache keyed on prompt fingerprints. For more advanced, Redwood Optimize suggests cache TTLs and when to use prefix vs full-result caching.
[00:05:30] Samir: Optimize — does that integrate with the console?
[00:05:33] Alex: Yes, Console has Optimize dashboards with batching suggestions, quantization recommendations, and telemetry per route. It surfaces cost tradeoffs too.
[00:05:43] Maya: I'll open the onboarding repo now and point to the quickstart file. Note: some of the function names in the SDK changed in beta -> stable, so watch the migration guide we include.
[00:05:56] [00:05:56] Maya: (shares link) https://github.com/redwood-inference/onboard-samples — sample apps in python/ts, GH workflow, and a vault example.
[00:06:10] Jordan: Nice. A couple network-specific questions: we run CI in an internal network without outbound egress except via a proxy. Any issues?
[00:06:19] Maya: Proxying is fine — you need to allow the proxy to reach our gateway on 443. If you require mutual TLS or a private connection, we can do dedicated peering.
[00:06:30] Priya: We also encrypt tokens with our KMS — can Redwood accept rotated keys or integrate with our KMS?
[00:06:36] Alex: We don't ingest your KMS keys; instead you store secrets in your KMS and provide Redwood only the token material. For auditability we support audit logs and can integrate with your SIEM via our logs export.
[00:06:49] Samir: On compliance: SOC2 docs and a whitepaper would be helpful.
[00:06:54] Alex: I'll attach the SOC2 and ISO docs in the follow-up.
[00:06:58] Maya: Back to code — I'll run the Python smoke test. Running: python smoke.py — it sends a small prompt to the sandbox model.
[00:07:06] [00:07:06] (key typing sounds)
[00:07:12] Maya: Response returned, about 150ms in sandbox for this short prompt. In prod you'd see different latency profiles based on model and sequence length.
[00:07:22] Jordan: 150ms — that's promising. We'll run a small benchmark later.
[00:07:27] Maya: For benchmarking, we recommend using our per-route profiling tool in Console and also capturing end-to-end latencies from your app. We can provide a spreadsheet template.
[00:07:38] Priya: Ok on secrets, for GH Actions we'll reference REDWOOD_API_KEY from secrets but for ephemeral tokens we'll have a serverless mint endpoint that uses the long-lived key stored in Vault.
[00:07:49] Maya: Exactly, that's the recommended pattern. It also avoids exposing the long-lived key in many places.
[00:07:55] Jordan: Any gotchas with TypeScript types? We've had mismatches before.
[00:07:59] Maya: The package exports types; if you pin to a major version you should be fine. We also publish a types-only package in case you want zero runtime.
[00:08:08] Samir: For the pilot, we want to test three flows: summarize docs, chat assistant, and batch embeddings. Does Redwood support embeddings in the same SDK?
[00:08:17] Alex: Yes, same SDK call surface with different endpoints: client.embeddings.create(...). We also offer reranking and semantic search helpers.
[00:08:26] Maya: I'll add sample embeddings scripts to the pilot folder.
[00:08:30] [00:08:30] Jordan: How does pricing for embeddings compare?
[00:08:34] Alex: Cost depends on model; embedding units are billed separately. We'll include cost-per-1k example numbers in the follow-up.
[00:08:42] Maya: Quick note on batching — you can batch multiple inputs into a single request; the SDK will flatten and unflatten responses for you. This saves token overhead.
[00:08:51] Priya: Will batching affect latency SLAs?
[00:08:55] Maya: It can increase per-request latency but decreases per-unit cost. That's why Optimize has workload-aware batching recommendations based on your latency SLOs.
[00:09:06] Alex: Let's quickly discuss rollout policies — our Console supports canary and A/B rollouts. You can route a percentage of traffic to a new model variant.
[00:09:17] Jordan: Helpful. We need a rollback mechanism if quality drops.
[00:09:20] Maya: Console supports automatic fallback to previous model or a cheaper fallback model on errors or latency breaches.
[00:09:28] Samir: For pilot timeline, we aim for a 2-week PoC starting next Monday. Can Redwood support that?
[00:09:33] Alex: Yes, that's reasonable. We'll provide sandbox keys and a test plan.
[00:09:38] Maya: I'll draft the test plan with specific eval prompts and pass/fail gates for quality and latency.
[00:09:45] Priya: Do you have a checklist for security review? We have a procurement window next month.
[00:09:50] Alex: Yes — SOC2/ISO, SSO/SAML, RBAC notes, audit logs, and data retention policies. I'll include that in the follow-up packet.
[00:09:59] [00:09:59] (brief silence)
[00:10:05] Maya: One more live example — showing env var rotation script: we have a helper that calls the Redwood token exchange and writes new token to Vault.
[00:10:16] Jordan: Nice. Could we see the CI job that runs smoke tests post-deploy?
[00:10:20] Maya: Yes, GH Actions job 'smoke-test' runs the sample app with REDWOOD_API_KEY, hits a health-check route and asserts response schema.
[00:10:31] Priya: For observability, do you emit request IDs we can correlate to our logs?
[00:10:36] Alex: Every request includes an x-request-id header in responses and we can surface it in Console traces.
[00:10:44] Jordan: Great. A couple of items on troubleshooting: if we see 429s, what should we do?
[00:10:48] Maya: 429s indicate rate limits — for spikes you can request burst capacity or add retries with exponential backoff in the client. Our SDK has retry helpers.
[00:10:58] Samir: For dedicated capacity, what's the SLA?
[00:11:01] Alex: Dedicated comes with SLA-backed uptime and latency targets; exact numbers depend on contract tier. We'll include the SLA matrix in the follow-up.
[00:11:10] Maya: Wrapping up the demo: repo link, demo recording we'll share, and the sandbox keys (Alex will DM).
[00:11:18] Jordan: Thanks — one last question: any data residency options for EU-only datasets?
[00:11:23] Alex: Yes, we have regionally-hosted endpoints and Private deployments for strict residency. We'll list region options in the doc.
[00:11:31] Priya: Ok thanks, that covers the major questions.
[00:11:35] Alex: Final recap — Redwood to send: onboarding repo, SOC2/ISO pack, allowlist IPs, sandbox keys, and test plan. Customer to validate egress rules and confirm pilot scope.
[00:11:46] Samir: Sounds good. We'll aim to have egress checks done by Thursday.
[00:11:49] Maya: I'll schedule the 30m CI integration follow-up for next week.
[00:11:53] Alex: Great — thanks everyone.
[00:11:55] (call ends)
